findings.title: join() can skip terminate() for multiple flusher subprocesses on timeout
findings.body: In join(), the per-process loop does `if deadline is not None: remaining_time = deadline - time.time(); if remaining_time <= 0: break`. Once the overall deadline has elapsed (e.g. because an earlier process took a while to die, or next_step.join(timeout) already consumed most of the timeout), the loop breaks immediately for that process and all subsequent processes in `self.processes`, so `process.terminate()` (line 346-347) is never called for them. In the old single-process implementation, terminate() was called unconditionally after the wait loop regardless of the deadline. Now, with multiple flusher processes, a timed-out join() can leave one or more child processes running and un-terminated after join() returns (e.g. during partition rebalance), potentially continuing to read Redis and produce segments for shards the consumer no longer owns, which can cause duplicate/late segment production to Kafka and resource leaks.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag key ('shard' vs 'shards') fragments flusher metrics
findings.body: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` are tagged with `tags={"shard": shard_tag}` (lines 185, 195), but `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` is tagged with `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` (line 199). This inconsistent tag key means the two related timers will produce separate, inconsistently-named tag dimensions in the metrics backend, breaking dashboards/alerts that expect a uniform 'shard' tag across these flusher metrics, especially important now that this PR is specifically introducing per-shard-process observability.

findings.title: `max_processes or len(...)` silently discards an explicit 0, and CLI option allows invalid values
findings.body: `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` uses `or`, so an explicitly passed `max_processes=0` is treated the same as `None` and silently replaced by one-process-per-shard instead of being honored or rejected. Additionally, the new `--flusher-processes` click option in src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py (around lines 432-437) has no `min=1` validation, so a negative value causes `self.num_processes = min(max_processes, len(shards))` to become negative; `range(negative_number)` yields an empty dict for `process_to_shards_map`, and the subsequent `self.process_to_shards_map[process_index].append(shard)` assignment then raises an unhandled `KeyError` at consumer startup rather than a clear configuration error.

findings.title: Unused dead code: `_create_process_for_shard`
findings.body: `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard: int)` (singular) is defined but never called anywhere in the class; all restart paths (`_ensure_processes_alive`) call `_create_process_for_shards` (plural) directly with the process_index and full shard list. This leftover method suggests an incomplete refactor (e.g. an intended per-shard-only restart path that was dropped) and should either be wired up or removed to avoid confusing maintainers.

findings.title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op due to earlier global monkeypatch, defeating its purpose
findings.body: The test patches the global `time.sleep` with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` at the top of the test. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` call (with comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change') therefore also resolves to the same no-op lambda, since monkeypatch replaces the attribute on the shared `time` module used by both the test and the flusher's background thread. The intended 100ms wall-clock wait never happens, so the test's correctness now relies on incidental GIL/thread-scheduling timing rather than a deterministic wait, which can make the test flaky under CI load despite the comment implying a real wait was added to fix flakiness.

findings.title: New multiprocess test only checks shard→process bookkeeping, not actual flush behavior
findings.body: `test_flusher_processes_limit` only asserts on `flusher.processes`, `flusher.max_processes`, `flusher.num_processes`, and `flusher.process_to_shards_map` sizes; it never submits any spans and never asserts that segments assigned to different shards (handled by different threads/processes) are actually flushed and produced correctly. This leaves the core new feature of this PR — correct end-to-end flushing when more than one flusher process/thread is active — without a test that exercises actual data flow and verifies correctness across multiple processes.
